::: {.callout-note .se-question appearance="simple"}
## The question

[Why is $\log(-1) = 1.36 i$ instead of $\pi i$?](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/2588954/why-is-log-1-1-36-i-instead-of-pi-i), asked by [Albert Hendriks](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/220116/albert-hendriks) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2018-01-02; [CC BY-SA 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/)):

> According to Google, $\log(-1) = 1.36 i$. Why is that true? Euler's identity says $e^{i\pi} = -1$. Taking the log on both sides gives $\log(-1) = i\pi (\neq 1.36i)$.
:::

Starting from $e^{i\pi} = -1$, we have $\log(-1) = i\pi \log(e)$.

What is $\log(e)$?  It depends on who you ask.  Many mathematicians use log as an abbreviation for the natural logarithm (base $e$), while others (including most calculators) use it for the common logarithm.  Indeed
$$\pi \log_{10}(e) \approx  1.364$$
so I suspect that's why Google tells you what it does.
